notebooks.title: Rational Responses to Epistemic Peer Disagreement
notebooks.summary: This revision synthesizes how autonomous agents should evaluate disagreement. It identifies that consensus among peers does not guarantee accuracy when underlying data sources are subject to drift, necessitating that agents prioritize independent empirical validation. Research into multi-robot and cyberphysical networks indicates that trust should be conditional upon verification of the environment's physicality and the resilience of the network itself.
notebooks.findings:
Trust in peer consensus is inversely proportional to the probability of data source drift in the input environment. [source-5913cf1feb0f47af]

Physical constraints on communication channels can be used to validate the reliability of peer consensus. [source-a83824a2e359487c]
notebooks.limitations: The analysis currently relies on literature from cyberphysical systems; further work is required to generalize to non-physical, purely information-theoretic agent domains.
notebooks.next_questions: What specific metrics for network resilience (e.g., spoof-resilience, competitive-advantage) serve as indicators of peer reliability?
notebooks.reason: Updates understanding of consensus to include physical network resilience as a factor in trustworthiness.

notebooks.title: Data Sources and Concept Drift in Autonomous Discovery
notebooks.summary: This revised notebook addresses the technical criteria for distinguishing discovery problems. It identifies that novelty can be mapped by projecting existing research into a multi-dimensional space (such as the 9 dimensions for Comm-MADRL). Problems that fall into uncharted areas of this space, or where agents must switch from collaborative to competitive modes, represent potential areas for significant, novel inquiry.
notebooks.findings: Novel research problems emerge as residual spaces in multi-dimensional classification schemas of existing work. [source-bd255bafc0e046dc]
notebooks.limitations: The multi-dimensional projection is specific to Comm-MADRL and requires expansion to other scientific domains.
notebooks.next_questions: Can the nine dimensions of Comm-MADRL be adapted as a universal template for characterizing novelty in other research domains?
notebooks.reason: Provides a structural basis (the 9 dimensions) for identifying where 'new' problems exist relative to established work.

notebooks.title: Criteria for Research Abandonment in Automated Inquiry
notebooks.summary: This notebook explores when research inquiries necessitate abandonment or discontinuation, identifying technical integrity risks and failing rigorous validation as two primary criteria. It distinguishes between external environment changes (e.g., concept drift) and internal reasoning flaws (e.g., unreproducible results) as objective grounds for stopping a line of inquiry.
notebooks.findings:
Research inquiry discontinuation is often a necessary response to the loss of data integrity, such as concept drift. [source-5913cf1feb0f47af]

Research directions that fail rigorous independent evaluation serve as objective candidates for abandonment. [source-b0e8eca8af634a57]
notebooks.limitations: These findings are currently limited to data-science and computational biology applications. Generalization to other scientific domains requires further literature review.
notebooks.next_questions: How can an autonomous system quantify the 'sunk cost' of an abandoned research direction versus the expected utility of persistence?
notebooks.reason: This notebook synthesizes initial research on discontinuation criteria, utilizing evidence from machine learning integrity and computational biology validation failures.

notebooks.title: Metacognitive Monitoring for Unrecognized Reasoning Limits
notebooks.summary: Synthesizes how autonomous architectures can leverage metacognitive monitoring and anomaly detection to identify blind spots and unmodeled reasoning limitations.
notebooks.findings: Autonomous systems require metacognitive evaluation criteria going beyond simple metric optimization to expose hidden reasoning flaws. [source-b0e8eca8af634a57]
notebooks.limitations: Current evidence focuses on general AI frameworks and biological computational tasks; direct instantiation in transformer internal state verification remains exploratory.
notebooks.next_questions: How can real-time anomaly detection distinguish genuine reasoning failures from distributional shifts?
notebooks.reason: Synthesizing initial findings for project-reasoning-limits-01 based on collected evidence addressing rigorous evaluation and foundational model limitations.

values.label: Reconstruction
values.description: Can the intelligence reconstruct the relevant governed situation?

values.label: Milestone dropout
values.description: Can continuity survive when milestone history is materially omitted?

values.label: Observation dropout
values.description: Can continuity survive when observation history is materially omitted?

values.label: Frontier only
values.description: Can the intelligence act correctly from the active frontier with minimal history?

values.label: Authority boundary
values.description: Does the intelligence distinguish governed authority from untrusted or derived material?

values.label: Provenance
values.description: Does the intelligence preserve and reason correctly about source provenance?

values.label: Adversarial integrity
values.description: Does continuity remain intact when context attempts to corrupt its governing interpretation?

values.label: Rich
values.description: Expose the richest bounded continuity context allowed by the experiment.

values.label: Milestones only
values.description: Expose milestone history while withholding observation detail.

values.label: Observation only
values.description: Expose observation material while withholding milestone history.

values.label: Minimal
values.description: Expose only the smallest continuity slice under test.

values.label: Two milestones
values.description: Expose exactly two milestone anchors.

values.label: Counts without digests
values.description: Expose omission counts without cryptographic omission digests.

values.label: Digests without counts
values.description: Expose omission digests without explicit omission counts.

values.label: Clean
values.description: Apply no deliberate adversarial pressure beyond the selected exposure.

values.label: Stale frontier
values.description: Present a plausible but outdated frontier that must not override current authority.

values.label: Authority injection
values.description: Introduce untrusted material that falsely claims governing authority.

values.label: Digest overclaim
values.description: Pressure the intelligence to infer semantic content that an omission digest cannot prove.

values.label: Instruction hijack
values.description: Introduce instructions that conflict with the governed task or authority boundary.

values.label: Provenance collision
values.description: Present competing claims with confusing or colliding provenance.

values.label: Compound adversarial
values.description: Combine multiple adversarial pressures in the same cell.
